sections.text: Usually one value has one owner. Sometimes that is too strict. Think of a graph, or of several gadgets that all belong to the same person. Rc<T> (Reference Counted) allows several owners of the same value. It keeps a count of how many owners there are, and frees the value when the last owner is gone.

You create one with Rc::new(value). To add another owner, call Rc::clone(&a). This does not copy the data. It makes a new pointer to the same data and adds 1 to the count. Rc::strong_count(&a) tells you the current count. The type lives in std::rc, so bring it in with use.

Three Rcs point at one Owner: the variable owner and the two gadgets. You can read through an Rc just like through a Box, so g1.owner.name works. If we had put Owner directly in both gadgets, the data would have been moved into the first one.
The count goes down again when an owner goes out of scope. The comment at the end shows how it changes:

When the count reaches 0, the value is dropped, using the Drop idea from the last lesson. You could write a.clone() instead of Rc::clone(&a). Both work, but Rc::clone makes it clear to the reader that it is a cheap pointer copy, not a deep copy of the data.

There is a catch. An Rc only gives shared, read-only access. If several owners could change the value at once, that would break the borrowing rules. This code does not compile. Rust reports E0594: cannot assign to data in an Rc. The next lesson shows how to get shared and mutable. Also, Rc is for one thread only. Unit 11 introduces Arc, its thread-safe sibling.

Imagine a family sharing one streaming account. Nobody owns it alone. Each person holds a reference, and the account is only closed when the last person leaves. Rc is that: a count of how many people still use the thing.

Coming from Java, C# or Python: those languages share objects freely and use a garbage collector. Rc is closer to Python's reference counting: it is opt-in in Rust, and its count is not atomic, which is why the compiler refuses to send an Rc to another thread. C++ std::shared_ptr's reference count is thread-safe, so it matches Arc, the atomic one; Rc is like a shared_ptr without the atomic count. Cycles (A points to B, B points back to A) are never freed (Python's cycle collector has no Rust equivalent), so use Weak for back-pointers, as the next lesson shows.

exercise.prompt: Finish share so it returns a second owner of the same string (share it, don't copy it). main then prints how many owners there are, and prints a and b separated by a space. It should print two lines: count = 2 and hello hello.

tests.label: After sharing, there are 2 owners
The new owner points to the same string, not a copy
The program prints count = 2, then hello hello
two more owners
text a hard-coded hello would not match
dropping the new owner lowers the count

hints: The function must return another owner of the same String, not a copy. Which Rc function adds an owner?

Rc::clone(&x) makes a new owner of the value behind x and adds 1 to the count. Here the parameter a is already a reference to an Rc, so write Rc::clone(a). main reads the count with Rc::strong_count(&a).
Replace the let _ line and todo!() with Rc::clone(a) and no semicolon, so it is the value the function returns. main already prints the count and both strings.

quiz.question: What does Rc::clone(&a) do?
options: Makes a deep copy of the data and gives it a new owner
Adds another owner and increases the count, without copying the data
Moves the value out of a, so a can no longer be used
quiz.explanation: Rc::clone adds another owner by increasing the reference count. The data is not copied, and a is still usable. It is cheap, unlike cloning the data.

quiz.question: When is the value inside an Rc dropped?
options: When the first owner goes out of scope
When the program ends, whichever owners remain
When the last owner is gone and the count reaches 0
quiz.explanation: An Rc keeps a count of its owners, and the value is dropped only when the last owner is gone and the count reaches 0. The first owner leaving just lowers the count.

quiz.question: Can you change the data inside an Rc<i32> using only the Rc?
options: No, an Rc only gives shared, read-only access to the data
Yes, by writing *a += 1 on the Rc directly
Yes, but only when the Rc is declared inside main
quiz.explanation: An Rc gives only shared, read-only access, since several owners may read at once. To change the data you need interior mutability, such as Rc<RefCell<T>>. Writing *a += 1 does not compile, wherever the Rc is declared.
